newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt ruling party challenges itself in elections.
newsitem.headline: Egypt ruling party challenges itself in elections.

text.p: Voting booths in Egypt's local elections closed on Monday with National Democratic Party (NDP) candidates left to compete against each other as oppositon parties fielded little challenge.

Unlike the 1992 local and provincial elections, when Islamist candidates posed a real threat to the government, NDP candidates held sway thanks to police round ups of Moslem fundamentalist candidates ahead of the vote.
The large Wafd party withdrew from the elections several weeks ago, citing its displeasure with the way elections were conducted and expressing doubts that the vote would be fair.
Other parties such as the Ahrar and Nasserite parties have fielded a small number of candidates.

According to government figures released last week the NDP had won at least 50 percent of the 47,382 municipal council seats without a vote being cast because there were not enough opposition or independent candidates contesting them.
Some candidates, including members of the NDP, accused the ruling party of rigging the vote to ensure victory.
"NDP men are rigging the elections," said Ahmed Mohamed Abdul-Meguid, a member of the NDP who was running as an independent candidate. "They are stuffing the ballot boxes."
Abdul-Meguid, other independent candidates and local people said police had rounded up several Islamist candidates in their Darb el-Ahmar constituency, a traditionally Islamist stronghold.
"They arrested all bearded youths in the area," he said.
The allegation was confirmed by a member of the pro-Islamist Socialist Labour Party (SLP), which fielded independents.
"They arrested Ali Salem, SLP secretary in the south suburb of Maasara, and the SLP official Ismail Abdul Tawab," SLP member Mohamed Abdul-Hamid Barakat told Reuters.

Police arrested 27 people including five journalists and a lawyer on Friday on suspicion of belonging to the outlawed and influential Moslem Brotherhood and using the election to spread the group's ideology.
Brotherhood spokesman Mamoun Hudaibi brushed aside the elections as a useless exercise.
"Elections! What elections? They are useless and we have considered them dead," Hudaibi told Reuters.
The independent rights group the Professional Unions Coordination Committee issued a report on voting in the northern province of Dakahliya headlined "the NDP versus the NDP".
A Reuter correspondent saw a voting booth official at one constituency show a voter which names to tick on his form.
Independent candidates said in the run up to the election that security officials had put them under pressure to withdraw to make way for NDP candidates.

Abdul-Moneim Fouad told Reuters by telephone from Medinet el-Salam, northwest of Cairo, that the head of the city council there and other local officials tried to crash into his car and stoned it during his campaign to prevent him from running.
"Security officials warned all independent candidates they would spray them with acid if they did not withdraw," he said.
He said the local education authority where he works decided to move him because he was running as an independent candidate.
Some candidates said low voter turnout was helping the NDP.
"Voter turnout is not more than seven percent," said Tagammu's Abdul-Salam. NDP members, who were distributing candy at voting booths, put turnout at between 40-50 percent.
Government newspapers said final results were expected by Tuesday.
